questions.q: Under Article 74, the President of India is generally bound to act on the:
o: Advice of the Chief Justice of India
Aid and advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister
Advice of the Vice-President alone
Advice of individual Members of Parliament
questions.src: Article 74 establishes that the President acts on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers, the core feature of India's Parliamentary system.

questions.q: A "Money Bill," under Article 110, may originate ONLY in:
o: The Rajya Sabha
The Lok Sabha
Either House equally
A joint sitting of both Houses
questions.src: Money Bills can only be introduced in the Lok Sabha; the Rajya Sabha's role is limited to recommendations within 14 days.

questions.q: The Governor of a State is:
o: Directly elected by the people of the State
Appointed by the President of India, holding office during the President's pleasure
Elected by the State Legislative Assembly
Appointed by the Chief Minister
questions.src: Unlike the President (elected indirectly by an Electoral College), the Governor is appointed by the President.

questions.q: Under the Seventh Schedule, if there is a conflict between a Union law and a State law on a Concurrent List subject, generally:
o: The State law always prevails
The Union (Central) law generally prevails, subject to specific exceptions under Article 254
Both laws are automatically void
The matter must always go to the Supreme Court before either law applies
questions.src: Article 254 establishes the general rule of Union law supremacy on Concurrent List conflicts, with narrow exceptions.

questions.q: In S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), the Supreme Court held that a Presidential Proclamation under Article 356 is:
o: Completely immune from any judicial review whatsoever
JUSTICIABLE — courts can examine whether it was based on relevant material and not mala fide
Only reviewable by the President personally
Automatically valid once issued, with no possibility of challenge
questions.src: Bommai established that Article 356 proclamations are subject to judicial review on these specific grounds, though not the adequacy of material.

questions.q: Following S.R. Bommai, the majority/confidence of a State Government must be tested:
o: Through the Governor's personal subjective assessment alone
On the FLOOR of the Legislative Assembly
Only through a public opinion poll
By the President without any Assembly involvement
questions.src: Bommai mandated that a floor test in the Assembly, not the Governor's subjective opinion, is the proper way to determine a government's majority.

questions.q: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India held that which TWO principles are part of the Constitution's Basic Structure?
o: Only judicial review
Federalism AND Secularism
Only the right to property
Only Parliamentary sovereignty
questions.src: Bommai extended Basic Structure protection to both federalism and secularism, a frequently overlooked dual holding.

questions.q: The Supreme Court's appellate jurisdiction via "Special Leave Petition" is exercised under:
o: Article 32
Article 136
Article 226
Article 356
questions.src: Article 136 grants the Supreme Court discretionary power to grant special leave to appeal from any court/tribunal in India.

questions.q: Article 226 (High Court writ jurisdiction), as compared to Article 32 (Supreme Court writ jurisdiction), is generally considered:
o: Narrower, covering only Fundamental Rights
BROADER — covering enforcement of Fundamental Rights AND "any other purpose" (ordinary legal rights too)
Identical in every respect
Not applicable to Fundamental Rights at all
questions.src: Article 226's "any other purpose" language gives High Courts a wider writ jurisdiction than the Supreme Court's Article 32.

questions.q: The "Collegium" system of judicial appointments (CJI plus four senior-most Supreme Court judges) was clarified in which case?
o: S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (First Judges Case, 1981)
In re Presidential Reference (Third Judges Case, 1998)
Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)
Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017)
questions.src: The Third Judges Case (1998) specifically clarified the Collegium's composition as the CJI plus the four senior-most judges.

questions.q: In the First Judges Case (S.P. Gupta v. Union of India, 1981), the Supreme Court held that "consultation" under Article 124:
o: Meant "concurrence," giving the judiciary primacy
Did NOT mean "concurrence," giving the Executive greater primacy in appointments
Was irrelevant to judicial appointments
Applied only to High Court appointments, never the Supreme Court
questions.src: The First Judges Case initially gave the Executive greater say by holding consultation did not require concurrence — a position later reversed.

questions.q: In Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India (2015, the "Fourth Judges Case"), the Supreme Court:
o: Upheld the NJAC Act as constitutional
By a 4:1 majority, struck down the NJAC Act and 99th Amendment as unconstitutional, preserving the Collegium
Abolished the Collegium system entirely with no replacement
Transferred all appointment power to Parliament
questions.src: The Fourth Judges Case struck down the NJAC as violating judicial independence (a Basic Structure feature), preserving the Collegium.

questions.q: The National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC), struck down in 2015, was introduced by which constitutional amendment?
o: The 42nd Amendment
The 99th Amendment
The 44th Amendment
The 73rd Amendment
questions.src: The 99th Constitutional Amendment 2014 created the NJAC, later struck down alongside the amendment itself.

questions.q: A National Emergency under Article 352 may be proclaimed on grounds of:
o: Any political disagreement between Centre and State
War, external aggression, or armed rebellion
A simple economic downturn
Only a natural disaster
questions.src: Article 352 restricts National Emergency grounds to these three specific categories, narrowed by the 44th Amendment.

questions.q: The 44th Amendment 1978 changed the ground of "internal disturbance" (Article 352) to:
o: "Economic crisis"
"Armed rebellion" — narrowing the ground following criticism of the 1975 Emergency's misuse
"Foreign interference"
The ground was removed entirely with no replacement
questions.src: This change was a direct, deliberate response to the widely-criticised misuse of "internal disturbance" during the 1975-77 Emergency.

questions.q: During a National Emergency, which Fundamental Rights CANNOT be suspended, even by Presidential Order?
o: All Fundamental Rights can be suspended without exception
Articles 20 and 21 (protection against ex-post-facto laws/double jeopardy/self-incrimination, and life/personal liberty)
Only Article 19
Only Article 32
questions.src: Articles 20 and 21 enjoy absolute protection from suspension, even during a National Emergency, following the 44th Amendment's reforms.

questions.q: "President's Rule" under Article 356 is proclaimed when:
o: The President simply dislikes a particular State government
The President is satisfied that a State's government cannot be carried on in accordance with constitutional provisions
A State loses a cricket match
A State government requests voluntary dissolution for any reason
questions.src: Article 356 requires a genuine breakdown of constitutional machinery, not mere political disagreement — a principle reinforced by Bommai.

questions.q: "Financial Emergency" under Article 360, in India's constitutional history to date, has been:
o: Invoked multiple times
NEVER invoked, remaining a purely theoretical provision so far
Invoked exactly once, in 1991
Automatically triggered every budget cycle
questions.src: Article 360 has never been formally proclaimed in India, unlike Articles 352 and 356, which have been invoked multiple times.

questions.q: The Anti-Defection Law is contained in which Schedule of the Constitution?
o: Seventh Schedule
Tenth Schedule, added by the 52nd Amendment 1985
Ninth Schedule
First Schedule
questions.src: The Tenth Schedule (52nd Amendment 1985) governs disqualification for defection from a political party.

questions.q: Under the Anti-Defection Law, a member is generally disqualified if they:
o: Simply disagree privately with their party's policy
Voluntarily give up party membership, or vote/abstain against a party whip without prior permission (subject to specified exceptions)
Ask a question in Parliament
Take leave of absence for illness
questions.src: The Tenth Schedule targets specific defection-related conduct, not mere policy disagreement or ordinary parliamentary activity.

questions.q: Most Indian State Legislatures are:
o: Bicameral (Assembly + Council) in every single state
UNICAMERAL (Legislative Assembly only) — only a handful of states retain a Legislative Council
Tricameral, with three houses
Entirely appointed, with no elected members
questions.src: Most states have only a Legislative Assembly; a small number (e.g., Telangana, UP, Bihar, Maharashtra, Karnataka) retain a Legislative Council under Article 169.

questions.q: The Supreme Court's ORIGINAL jurisdiction under Article 131 covers:
o: Only criminal appeals from High Courts
Disputes between the Union and States, or between States themselves
Only matters relating to Fundamental Rights
Only election disputes
questions.src: Article 131 gives the Supreme Court exclusive original jurisdiction over Centre-State and inter-State disputes.

questions.q: The Inter-State Council, under Article 263, primarily serves to:
o: Replace the Supreme Court in Centre-State disputes
Inquire into and advise on disputes between States, or matters of common interest to the Union and States
Appoint State Governors
Control State budgets directly
questions.src: The Inter-State Council is an advisory body facilitating cooperative federalism, distinct from judicial dispute resolution.

questions.q: The Goods and Services Tax (GST) framework, restructuring Centre-State financial relations, was introduced by which constitutional amendment?
o: The 42nd Amendment
The 101st Amendment 2016
The 44th Amendment
The 86th Amendment
questions.src: The 101st Amendment 2016 introduced GST, creating a shared Union-State indirect tax framework administered via the GST Council.

questions.q: "Collective Responsibility" of the Council of Ministers to the Lok Sabha means that:
o: Each minister is individually accountable only to the Prime Minister
The entire Council of Ministers must resign if it loses the confidence/majority of the Lok Sabha
Ministers are never accountable to Parliament at all
Only the Prime Minister, not the full Council, bears any responsibility
questions.src: Collective responsibility means the whole Council stands or falls together based on Lok Sabha confidence, a core Parliamentary-system feature.
